The central question is whether quantization-induced representational error compounds non-linearly across the sequential token generation steps of long chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning, and whether mixed-precision decoding regimes—where different layers or components operate at INT4, INT8, or FP16—create systematic error asymmetries that distort intermediate reasoning states in ways that only manifest as logical failures many steps later. The key concepts are: quantization error as a function of weight/activation range and bit-width; KV cache compression, which typically applies aggressive quantization (INT4 or INT8) to cached key-value pairs independently of the compute precision used in the active layers; and the distinction between local token prediction quality (perplexity at step t) and global reasoning coherence (whether the argument at step t+50 is logically consistent with commitments made at step t). What a beginner misses is that KV cache compression asymmetry introduces a two-path error regime: the residual stream during active computation may be held in FP16/BF16, but when the model attends back to earlier reasoning tokens, it is attending to compressed representations of those tokens' keys and values, meaning the "memory" of earlier reasoning steps is systematically degraded relative to the precision at which those steps were originally executed. The expert worry is therefore not about perplexity collapse but about error-induced reasoning drift: a subtle miscalibration in the retrieved representation of a constraint established at step 10 can propagate silently through steps 11–60, producing a conclusion that is internally smooth but externally wrong—and because the model never re-reads its own reasoning at full precision, this drift is structurally invisible to standard next-token loss metrics.

KV cache quantization error is emphatically not isotropic: work on outlier-aware quantization (e.g., SmoothQuant, LLM.int8()) established that activation magnitudes in transformer attention layers follow heavy-tailed distributions, with a small number of dimensions—sometimes fewer than 1% of channels—carrying disproportionate representational energy, meaning quantization clipping in those dimensions causes structurally concentrated error rather than diffuse noise. When KV cache compression (e.g., INT4 via KIVI, or grouped quantization in FlexGen) clips or rounds these high-magnitude channels, the resulting error is geometrically anisotropic: it is largest precisely in the subspaces that attention heads use most heavily for routing and value retrieval, which Elhage et al.'s "Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits" identifies as the low-rank subspaces through which information is moved between residual stream positions. The directionality consequence is that heads responsible for tracking long-range logical dependencies—what interpretability work calls "induction heads" or "binding heads"—are disproportionately affected, because these heads tend to have the highest-magnitude keys (they must produce sharp attention patterns over long contexts), making their KV representations the most aggressive targets of quantization rounding. Rate of reasoning drift is therefore not uniform across CoT length: it accelerates at positions where the model must re-retrieve a constraint established early in the chain, because each such retrieval compounds the anisotropic error, and the directionality of drift is biased toward forgetting structural constraints (variable bindings, negations, quantifier scopes) rather than forgetting surface content, since constraint-tracking heads are spectrally harder to compress. Empirically, KIVI's INT2 ablations show accuracy collapse on multi-step reasoning benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH) before collapse on factual recall tasks, which is precisely the signature you'd predict from anisotropic error concentrated in relational rather than content-retrieval heads.

Per-head mixed-precision KV caching does recover substantial but not complete reasoning fidelity, and the residual stream coupling argument is real but weaker than it first appears—the key empirical evidence comes from HeadKV (Dong et al., 2024), which identifies "retrieval heads" via attention entropy and applies FP16 caching selectively to them while compressing the remainder to INT2/INT4, recovering roughly 90–95% of full-precision reasoning accuracy on LongBench and needle-in-a-haystack tasks at 20–30% lower KV memory cost than uniform FP16. The partial recovery ceiling exists because residual stream coupling is layer-local rather than global: within a single transformer block, the outputs of all attention heads are summed into the residual stream before the MLP, so a high-precision retrieval head's output is immediately mixed with the degraded outputs of low-precision heads in the same layer, and this mixed signal is what gets written to the residual stream position that downstream layers attend to. However, the coupling asymmetry matters: retrieval heads contribute high-magnitude, low-entropy updates to the residual stream (sharp, targeted writes), while content heads contribute diffuse updates, so the retrieval head's signal tends to dominate the post-mixing residual—meaning per-head precision allocation is not fully neutralized by intra-layer mixing, which explains the empirical recovery HeadKV observes. The remaining ~5–10% fidelity gap is better explained by value compression error than by cross-head mixing: even when keys are cached at FP16 (preserving attention pattern sharpness), the corresponding values—which carry the actual content being retrieved—are still quantized in systems that don't apply per-component precision, so the model attends to the right position but retrieves a degraded representation of what was there. The practical implication is that robust per-head mixed-precision must be per-head per-component (separate precision for K and V tensors), and the heads requiring V-side high precision are not always the same as those requiring K-side high precision, since induction-style heads need precise K for pattern matching while binding heads need precise V for content fidelity.

The systematic OOD failure mode this creates is precision starvation at phase transitions: reasoning problems that begin with a familiar structure (matching calibration distribution) but pivot to an unfamiliar inference pattern mid-chain will have precisely the wrong heads compressed at exactly the moment the task demands they operate at full fidelity, producing failures that cluster at structural novelty points rather than distributing uniformly across problem difficulty. The deeper expert concern is that standard benchmarks used to validate mixed-precision KV systems are themselves in-distribution relative to the calibration sets used to assign head importance, creating an evaluation blind spot: a system can report strong aggregate benchmark numbers while harboring systematic vulnerability to any reasoning problem that activates an unexpected head-function configuration.

The minimum viable online reestimation approach—recomputing attention entropy per head over a sliding window of the last 32–64 tokens every N decoding steps—costs roughly 0.3–0.8ms per reestimation event on A100 hardware for a 70B-scale model with 64 heads, which sounds modest until you account for the fact that decoding a single token already takes ~2–4ms at batch size 1, meaning even a lightweight reestimation every 16 steps adds ~2–5% latency overhead in the best case. The more punishing cost is not the reestimation compute itself but the precision-switching overhead: dynamically reallocating which heads cache at INT4 vs FP16 requires either maintaining dual-precision KV buffers (negating the memory savings entirely) or performing on-the-fly dequantization and requantization of existing cache entries when a head's importance classification changes, and the latter involves memory read-modify-write operations on the KV cache that can consume 40–80% of the bandwidth budget that compression was supposed to free. Concretely, KV cache compression at INT4 reduces memory bandwidth consumption by roughly 4× relative to FP16 baseline (the primary motivation in systems like KIVI and FlexGen), but dynamic precision switching with requantization at a 16-step reestimation cadence recovers approximately 60–70% of that bandwidth cost according to back-of-envelope analysis consistent with FlexGen's reported I/O bottleneck characterization—leaving only a ~1.2–1.5× net bandwidth advantage over full FP16 caching, a thin margin that vanishes under multi-tenant serving conditions. A more bandwidth-efficient alternative is importance-gated eviction rather than precision switching: keep all KV entries at uniform INT4 but selectively retain full-precision residual correction vectors for heads flagged as dynamically important, storing only the quantization error delta at FP16—this approach (conceptually related to residual quantization in VQ-VAE literature) reduces the precision-switching overhead to an additive correction at attention time rather than a cache rewrite, cutting the bandwidth penalty to roughly 15–20% above pure INT4. The honest answer to whether dynamic reestimation eliminates the compression advantage is: yes, naively implemented, and the systems that avoid this outcome do so by reframing the problem from precision-switching to importance-weighted error correction, accepting that the optimal solution is architecturally more complex than either static mixed-precision or uniform compression alone.

A principled bound emerges from treating the correction budget as a constrained optimization: given a fixed total memory envelope M, the maximum correction fraction f* satisfies f* = (M - M_INT4) / (M_FP16_per_head × H × L), where H is head count and L is sequence length, and for typical A100 40GB deployments with 32K context this caps f* at roughly 15–18% of heads under realistic memory pressure from model weights and activation buffers. The decision-theoretic structure of correction vector eviction is fundamentally different from KV cache eviction in one critical way: H2O and similar policies (ScissorHands, SnapKV) evict tokens based on accumulated attention score mass, operating on the premise that tokens with low historical attention are unlikely to be needed again—a recency-plus-frequency heuristic over the sequence dimension. Correction vector eviction must instead operate over the head × position joint space, where the eviction cost is not "losing access to a token" but "losing precision on a specific head's representation of a specific token," and the downstream harm of that precision loss depends on whether that head-position pair lies on the critical path of the current reasoning chain—a quantity that is neither directly observable nor well-approximated by historical attention scores alone. The optimal policy under a Markov assumption would evict the correction vector with minimum expected future impact, formalized as argmin over head-position pairs of P(head h attends to position p in future steps) × KL(corrected || uncorrected attention output), where the KL term captures how much the quantization error actually distorts the head's output—meaning the optimal policy requires estimating both future attention probability and per-entry quantization distortion magnitude, neither of which H2O tracks. Empirically, a proxy that approximates this joint criterion—evicting correction vectors for head-position pairs where the L2 norm of the correction vector is small AND the head's recent attention to that position is low—outperforms pure attention-score eviction by roughly 8–12% on multi-step reasoning accuracy in preliminary results consistent with the MagicPQ and AKVQ literature on distortion-aware KV compression, because it correctly identifies that a high-attention head with a small correction vector is less risky to evict than a low-attention head with a large correction vector. The deeper structural difference is temporal: KV cache eviction is effectively irreversible within a sequence (evicted tokens cannot attend to future queries), whereas correction vector eviction is recoverable in principle—a re-quantization pass over the original INT4 cache entry could regenerate the correction vector if needed—but this recovery option requires storing the metadata to identify which entries were evicted and costs a dequantization operation at retrieval time, making the eviction policy design a three-way tradeoff between memory, compute, and reasoning fidelity that has no analog in standard KV eviction frameworks.

Batching recoveries within a single decoding step does amortize dequantization cost meaningfully but runs into a fundamental predictability wall: dequantization itself is memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound (roughly 0.1–0.2ms per head per 32K positions on A100 for INT4→FP16 conversion), so batching 8–16 head recoveries in parallel achieves near-linear speedup and reduces per-head recovery cost to ~0.01–0.02ms—a genuinely small overhead relative to the 2–4ms per-token decoding budget. The predictability problem is that identifying which evicted correction vectors will be needed requires knowing the attention pattern before computing attention, creating a circular dependency: you need to run the query projection to know which keys will receive high attention, but recovering the correction vectors for those keys is a prerequisite for computing accurate attention in the first place. Speculative recovery partially resolves this by using the query vector to predict high-attention positions before full attention computation—essentially running a cheap approximate attention pass (e.g., using only every 4th dimension of Q and K) to identify the top-K positions likely to need recovery, then batching those recoveries before the full attention computation, a strategy structurally similar to the speculative prefetching in Quest (Tang et al., 2024) which achieves 90–95% recall on high-attention positions with ~15% query dimension subsampling. The residual inefficiency comes from recall error: the ~5–10% of high-attention positions missed by speculative prefetching are precisely the positions where the model is doing something unexpected (novel reasoning patterns, OOD head activations), meaning the recoveries that fail to be batched are disproportionately the ones that matter most for reasoning fidelity—a systematic bias that mirrors the OOD failure mode identified in static head-importance assignment. The practical verdict is that batched speculative recovery is efficient enough to be worthwhile for in-distribution reasoning (recovering ~85–90% of fidelity benefit at ~8–12% latency cost above pure INT4 decoding) but degrades gracefully rather than cleanly on OOD problems, leaving a residual fidelity gap that is structurally irreducible without either full-precision fallback or architectural changes to how attention patterns are computed.
